html:
A small early medieval church in Rome, a short walk from Santa Maria Maggiore, dedicated to Saint Praxedes, who with her sister Pudentiana was said to have cared for persecuted Christians and buried martyrs against Roman law. A church stood near the site by the 5th century. The present one was laid out under Pope Hadrian I about 780 and rebuilt and decorated by Pope Paschal I, pope from 817 to 824, over the remains of a Roman bath. Paschal emptied the catacombs of martyrs' bones and brought many of them here, part of a building campaign in the years of the Carolingian revival under Charlemagne and his heirs. Paschal is buried in the church.

Paschal's mosaics are the reason to come. In the apse Christ stands between Peter and Paul, who present Praxedes and Pudentiana, and at the far left Paschal, with the square halo of a living man, offers a model of the church. On the arches above, the Lamb sits on a throne among the symbols of the four Gospel writers, and rows of figures with wreaths welcome the saved into heaven.

The Chapel of St Zeno, a small funeral chapel inside the church, was built by Paschal for his mother, Theodora, and filled with relics of Zeno and other martyrs; with the apse it holds the church's best known mosaics. One panel shows four women: Mary, Praxedes, Pudentiana, and Theodora with a square halo and the word episcopa, "bishop", a title scholars still argue over. The church also keeps a piece of a column said to be the one Christ was whipped against, brought from the Holy Land in 1223. Since 1198 the church has been served by Vallombrosan Benedictine monks.
